newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia bond ylds up again, rates hopes cracking.
newsitem.headline: Australia bond ylds up again, rates hopes cracking.

text.p: *Short Australian debt futures closed lower for the second consecutive session as confidence of a monetary policy easing next week continued to show signs of cracking.
*Bill futures just pricing in a 25 b.p. rate cut.
Short Australian bond and bill futures closed lower for the second consecutive session as confidence about a monetary policy easing next week continued to show signs of cracking.
And this time round, even long dated yields were starting to rise as hopes of a 50 basis point easing in current 5.5 percent official interest rates were being watered down.
"(The rate cut) timing is unsure. There's good grounds to think that it is going to be next week, or in the next five weeks," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.
The price downturn coincided with upbeat comments on future employment growth by Treasurer Peter Costello on Thursday.

"The ABS (Australian Bureau of Statistics) job vacancies data taken together with ANZ job vacancies series are supportive of a strengthening in relation to employment and employment prospects over coming months," Costello told Parliament.

The ABS jobs vacancies data released earlier on Thursday, and usually ignored by the market, showed an adjusted rise of 2.7 percent in the three months to May after a fall of 0.9 percent in the three months to February. May job vacancies were 7.7 percent higher than a year ago.
Rate cut expectations had been running high since the exteremly weak labour report two weeks ago and a 50 basis point cut had been seen as more or less a certainty after the July 1 RBA board meeting.
However, the meeting does clash with the Federal Open Market Committee meeting on July 1 and 2, and at the same time Australian retail trade data is due on July 2.

This apparent weakness of this sector of the economy had also led the market to believe that a rate cut was on the cards after the back to back negatives in the data series in March and April, the first seen for three years.
Retail trade should statistically rebound in May, but the market is wary about the size of the rise.
Citibank's Koukoulas said the RBA board may even want to see the inflation and wages data at the end of July and how the whole economy performs in that time frame.
The local market had held its ground against a late sell-off in U.S. Treasuries on Wednesday, but by the close, yield differentials were widening out again.

Local bonds even underperformed against the long New Zealand debt, which came under mild pressure after today's debut budget by the coalition government. Analysts said the budget showed more emphasis on spending, although reaction there was muted ahead of Friday's RBNZ monetary policy statement.
